cues.x: Grit, by Angela Duckworth.
I want to start you at West Point, on a July morning, because that is where this book starts and because the puzzle there is the whole book in miniature.

Every summer, about twelve hundred young Americans arrive at the United States Military Academy to begin what is officially called Cadet Basic Training and what everyone actually calls Beast Barracks.
Beast.
Getting there in the first place is extraordinarily hard.
You need top grades, top test scores, a record of athletic achievement, and a nomination from a member of Congress or the Vice President.
Roughly fourteen thousand young people start that application process each year.
About twelve hundred make it in.
These are, by any conventional measure, some of the most capable teenagers in the country.

And then, over seven weeks in the summer heat, they get up at five in the morning and they run and they march and they get yelled at, with no weekends, no visitors, no phones, no movies, no video games, and almost nothing that resembles fun.
Beast is deliberately designed as the hardest thing they have ever done.
And every year, one in five cadets drops out before graduation, with a big chunk of them quitting during that very first summer.
Kids who spent years of their lives fighting to get in, walking away within weeks.
Now, West Point is a serious institution with serious analysts, and they had built a serious tool to predict this.
It is called the Whole Candidate Score, and it combines your test scores, your high school rank, an assessment of leadership potential, and a physical fitness exam.
It is a genuinely good measure of talent.
And it did a fine job of predicting who would do well in classes and on the parade ground.
It did an almost useless job of predicting who would quit during Beast.
Fitness scores did not do it.
Test scores did not do it.
Nothing in the folder of accomplishments that got these kids admitted told you who would still be standing in August.
Angela Duckworth, then a graduate student in psychology, showed up with a questionnaire she had made herself.
It was twelve items long.
It took about three minutes.

It asked things like whether you finish whatever you begin, whether setbacks discourage you, whether new ideas and projects sometimes distract you from previous ones, whether you have been obsessed with a certain idea or project for a short time but later lost interest.
She called it the Grit Scale, and what it measured was not talent at all.
It measured whether you keep going, over years, on the same thing.
It predicted who would survive Beast.
Not perfectly, nothing does, but far better than the elaborate score West Point had built.
The kids who stayed were not the fittest, not the smartest, not the most decorated.
They were the grittiest.
And once Duckworth started looking, that pattern showed up everywhere she pointed the questionnaire.
At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, grit predicted which children advanced to the later rounds.
In Chicago public schools, grittier students were more likely to graduate.
Among rookie teachers dropped into the toughest schools in the country, the gritty ones were more likely to be there in June and their students learned more.
Among salespeople at a company with brutal turnover, grit was the single best predictor of who kept their job.
Among candidates for the Army Special Operations Forces, the Green Berets, at a selection course so hard that most people who show up do not finish, grit predicted completion.
So what is it?
Duckworth defines grit as passion and perseverance for very long-term goals.
Not intensity.
Stamina.
And she is careful about the word passion, because we usually use it to mean a burst of feeling, a fire, an infatuation.
That is not what she means at all.
She means something closer to abiding loyalty.
The gritty person is not the one who feels most excited about their work on a given Tuesday.
The gritty person is the one who is still working on the same thing five years later, and ten years later, having gotten a great deal better at it in the meantime.
To make the passion half concrete, Duckworth asks you to draw your goals as a pyramid.
At the bottom sit dozens of small, low-level goals: answer these emails, get to the gym today, finish this chapter.
Those are means, and they are meant to be swapped out freely when they stop working.
In the middle sit mid-level goals, which are the projects and roles those small actions serve.
And at the very top sits a single ultimate concern, a goal that is not a means to anything else.
It is the compass.
Everything below it exists to serve it.
The reason this diagram matters is that most people who describe themselves as hard working but scattered do not have a low-level goal problem.
They have a top-level goal problem.
They have three or four ultimate concerns, all pulling in different directions, and their pyramid is really three half-built pyramids sharing the same twenty four hours.
Gritty people, when you map them, have an unusually tall and unusually narrow structure.
Enormous variety at the bottom, one thing at the top, held for decades.
Duckworth tells a story here that she flags as possibly apocryphal but too useful to omit.
Warren Buffett is said to have told his personal pilot, who was frustrated at not achieving more, to write down the twenty five things he most wanted to accomplish in his career.
Then to circle the top five.

Then to look at the remaining twenty, the ones he still genuinely wanted, and treat them not as a someday list but as the list to avoid at all costs, because those are exactly the things attractive enough to steal time from the five that matter.
Whether or not the conversation happened, the psychology is exactly right.
The threat to a tall pyramid is almost never the obviously bad option.
It is the good one.
She is also careful to say that giving up on lower-level goals is not just permitted, it is required.
If a means is not serving the end, drop it and find another.
What gritty people do not do is give up on the thing at the top when a means fails.
A setback tells you the route was wrong.
It does not tell you the destination was wrong.
Most quitting confuses the two.
Before we go any further, you should know where this book came from, because it did not come out of nowhere.
Duckworth grew up with a father who, over dinner, apropos of very little, would announce to her, you know, you're no genius.
He was not being cruel exactly.
He was a chemist at DuPont, he cared enormously about intelligence, and he simply held the view that people are dealt a certain hand and that his daughter's hand was ordinary.
She spent a great deal of her childhood absorbing that.
And years later, after she had built this body of research on the primacy of effort over talent, she got a phone call telling her she had been awarded a MacArthur Fellowship.
The award everyone calls the genius grant.
She writes about the irony with real feeling, because by then her father had Parkinson's and could not fully register the news.
She had spent her life proving that genius is not the thing that matters, and got handed a genius award for it.
Her path to the work was equally unglamorous.
She went to Harvard, then Oxford, then to McKinsey as a management consultant, which is exactly the sort of career that impresses people at dinner parties.
She hated it.
She left, and she went and taught seventh grade math in New York City public schools.
And in that classroom she watched something that did not fit the story she had been raised on.
The students who did best in her class were not always the ones who picked things up fastest.
Some of her sharpest, quickest kids drifted and underperformed.
Some of the slower ones, the ones who had to work through a problem three times, kept turning up, kept redoing the work, and ended the year well ahead.
Aptitude, she realized, was not the same as achievement, and the gap between them was made of something nobody was measuring.
So at twenty seven she quit teaching and went to graduate school at the University of Pennsylvania, to study under Martin Seligman, to find out what that something was.
Now let me give you the core argument, because this is the intellectual heart of the book and it is stated as an equation, or rather two equations.
Talent times effort equals skill.
Skill times effort equals achievement.
Read those again slowly, because the punch is in the repetition.
Talent is how quickly your skills improve when you invest effort.
That is all it is.
It is a rate, not a destination.
Effort turns talent into skill.
And then effort, again, is what turns skill into actual accomplishment in the world.
Which means effort counts twice.
It appears in both equations.
Talent appears in only one.
This is not a motivational slogan.
It is a claim about arithmetic, and it explains a lot of what we all observe.
It explains the phenomenally gifted person who never quite produces anything, whose talent stayed talent and never became skill.
It explains the person of modest natural ability whose body of work is enormous, because they compounded ordinary gains over an extraordinary number of years.
And it explains why, in field after field, the people at the very top are not the ones who looked most promising at the start.
Duckworth then asks a question I found genuinely uncomfortable.
If effort matters this much, and it clearly does, why are we so obsessed with talent?
She goes to Nietzsche for the answer, who wrote about our worship of genius with real contempt.
His point was that when we call someone a natural, we let ourselves off the hook.
If a person's greatness is a gift from the gods, then their achievement is not a rebuke to us.
We do not have to compete with the sublime.
But if their greatness was built, brick by brick, over ten thousand ordinary days, then their existence raises a question about how we have spent our own days, and nobody enjoys that question.
Calling other people naturals is, in part, a kindness we do for ourselves.
There is a wonderful study on exactly this, by a researcher named Chia-Jung Tsay, herself a trained pianist.
She asked professional musicians, people with a decade or more of training, to listen to two short recordings of a pianist and judge which one had more potential for a professional career.
She told them one performer was a natural, someone whose ability had shown early and effortlessly, and that the other was a striver, someone who had gotten there through hard work and determination.
The musicians, when asked directly and in the abstract, all said that hard work matters more than innate talent.
That is what everyone says.
But when they actually judged the recordings, they preferred the natural.
They rated the natural as more likely to succeed and more hireable.
And here is the thing: the two recordings were the same person.
It was the same clip.
Only the story attached to it had changed.
Even experts, even people who consciously believe in the value of effort, carry a bias toward the myth of the natural.

If you want the antidote to that myth, Duckworth points at a piece of research from 1989 by a sociologist named Dan Chambliss, an ethnography of competitive swimmers that he called The Mundanity of Excellence.

Chambliss spent years around swimmers at every level, from local clubs up to Olympians, expecting to find that the great ones were doing something categorically different, some secret, some hidden gift.
What he found instead was that excellence is made of small, ordinary, unremarkable things done consistently and correctly.
A slightly better turn at the wall.
A slightly better body position off the blocks.
Showing up to the early practice.
Eating properly.
None of it magical.
Dozens of little skills, each of them learnable, each of them mundane, drilled until they are habitual, and then stacked.
Superlative performance, Chambliss concluded, is a confluence of dozens of small skills or activities.
Nothing extraordinary or superhuman about any one of them.
Only the fact that they are done consistently and correctly, and all together, produce excellence.
Duckworth loves this because it dissolves the mystery.
We call it talent because we did not see the ten thousand mornings.
All right.
So how does grit actually get built?
Duckworth's answer is that gritty people, whether they know it or not, develop four psychological assets, and they tend to develop them in this order: interest, practice, purpose, and hope.
I want to take each one properly, because this is the actionable part of the book.
The first is interest, and here Duckworth attacks one of the most-repeated pieces of career advice in the world: follow your passion.
Her objection is not that passion is unimportant.
Her objection is that the advice describes passion as something you find, like a set of keys you dropped, and that this is almost the opposite of how it actually works.
Passion is not discovered in a flash of certainty.
It is developed, slowly, usually over years, and it almost always begins with something much humbler than a calling.
It begins with a mild interest.
A thing that is a bit more interesting than the other things.
The research on how interests form, much of it by a psychologist named Ann Renninger, describes two stages.
First, triggering.
Something catches your attention, often accidentally, often in a context of play, often through a person who made it feel welcoming.
Then, deepening, which takes years, and which requires you to come back to the thing repeatedly, accumulate knowledge, and discover that the deeper you go the more interesting it becomes.
Novices need novelty.
Experts find nuance.
To a beginner, all wine tastes like wine, and the only way to get more interested is to try something else.
To an expert, one vineyard's output across two adjacent years contains a whole world of difference.
That is why long engagement is not the enemy of passion.
It is the mechanism of it.
This is why Duckworth says the most reliable thing you can do early on is not to agonize about your one true calling but to dabble deliberately.
Try things.
Follow up on the flickers.
Do not demand that a new interest announce itself with a trumpet blast, because it usually will not.
She points out that people rarely can tell you when their interest began with any precision, and that vocational interests do not typically stabilize until people are well into their twenties.
Julia Child did not discover food as a girl.
She was in her thirties, eating a plate of sole meunière in Rouen, when the door opened.
The instruction is not to wait for that plate of fish.
It is to keep eating in new restaurants.
The second asset is practice, and this is where Duckworth brings in the work of Anders Ericsson, the psychologist who spent his career studying how experts get to be experts.
The finding is that experts do not simply accumulate hours.
Ordinary practice, the kind where you do the thing you can already do reasonably well, produces almost nothing after a certain point.
There are people who have driven for forty years and are worse drivers than they were at twenty five.
What produces improvement is deliberate practice, and it has a specific and rather unpleasant shape.
You set a stretch goal, focused on one narrow aspect of your performance that is currently a weakness.
You give it your full and undivided attention.
You get immediate and honest feedback, usually about what you got wrong.
And then you repeat, with refinement, until the thing you could not do becomes automatic, at which point you go find the next thing you cannot do.
The critical part, the part most people skip, is the deliberate targeting of weakness.
Improvement lives in the part of the work you are worst at, which is precisely the part that is least fun to spend an afternoon on.
Duckworth quotes Rowdy Gaines, the American swimmer, who calculated that in the years leading up to the 1984 Olympics he swam something like twenty thousand miles in training.
Twenty thousand miles, in a pool, going back and forth, to race for forty nine seconds.
He said he did it because he loved to swim, and Duckworth believes him, but she also wants you to notice that loving it and finding it easy are not the same thing at all.
Which raises the objection everyone raises.
If practice is this unpleasant, why do the greats do so much of it?

Duckworth took that question directly to Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, the psychologist who discovered flow, that state of effortless absorption in which time disappears and performance feels spontaneous and joyful.
Flow and deliberate practice sound like exact opposites.
One is agony, one is bliss.
They had a public exchange about it, and Duckworth's resolution is elegant.
Deliberate practice is for preparation.
Flow is for performance.

The gritty expert spends most of their working hours in the uncomfortable, corrective, feedback-heavy mode, and then, on the day, in the competition or the concert or the surgery, all that preparation surfaces as something that looks and feels effortless.
The flow is real.
It is also earned, in a room where nobody was watching, doing the parts they were bad at.
She found this in her spelling bee data too.
She followed the finalists of the National Spelling Bee and asked them exactly how they prepared.
Some read for pleasure.
Some were quizzed by parents.
Some did solitary deliberate practice, which for a speller means sitting alone with flashcards, actively working on the words you do not know, in silence.
Guess which one predicted final ranking.
The solitary, effortful practice, and by a clear margin.
And when the children rated the activities, they consistently rated that same practice as the least enjoyable and the most effortful thing they did.
The grittiest kids did the most of it anyway.
Duckworth's practical advice here is to make it a ritual rather than a decision.
Same time, same place, every day, so that the willpower is spent on the work rather than on the question of whether to begin.
And she suggests reframing the discomfort.
Instead of treating a mistake as evidence that you lack the gift, treat it as the only information that tells you where to aim tomorrow.
The third asset is purpose, and this is what turns an interest into something that can hold you for decades.
Duckworth uses the old parable of the three bricklayers.
You ask each one what he is doing.
The first says, I am laying bricks.
The second says, I am building a church.
The third says, I am building the house of God.
Same job, same wall, same wage.
Three completely different relationships with the work.
The first has a job.
The second has a career.
The third has a calling.

That framing comes from research by Amy Wrzesniewski, who has studied how people relate to their work across all kinds of occupations, and one of her most striking findings is that the split between job, career and calling has surprisingly little to do with the job itself.
She found the whole range inside single professions, including among hospital cleaning staff.
Some custodians described themselves as cleaning rooms.

Others described themselves as part of the team that heals the patients, and they behaved accordingly, timing their work to avoid disturbing sleeping patients, rearranging the pictures on the walls in the rooms of people in long comas because it might help, talking to the families.
Same title, same pay, entirely different work.
Duckworth found that gritty people are far more likely to say their work is a calling and to describe it as connected to the wellbeing of others.
This matters for stamina in an obvious way.

Interest alone can carry you a long way, but when the work stops being fun, and it will, at some point, for everyone, the thing that keeps you at the desk is the sense that it matters to somebody beyond yourself.

Her best portrait of this is Kat Cole, who started as a hostess at a Hooters restaurant at seventeen, working to help support her family after her mother left an alcoholic husband with three girls and almost no money.
Cole ended up doing every job in the restaurant, because when the cooks walked out one night, she went into the kitchen.
When people needed training, she trained them.
At nineteen she was flying to Australia to open franchises, without ever having been on a plane.
She dropped out of college to keep going, which she does not present as a general recommendation, and eventually became president of Cinnabon before she was thirty five.
What Duckworth wants you to see is not the speed of the rise.
It is that Cole consistently interpreted her work in terms of the people it served, and that this interpretation is available to almost anyone, in almost any job, right now.
Because purpose is not only found by changing careers.
Duckworth points out three practical routes.
You can reflect on how the work you already do contributes to something beyond you, which is often true and rarely noticed.
You can make small changes to your existing work that better connect it to your core values, which Wrzesniewski calls job crafting.
And you can find a purposeful role model, someone who demonstrates that this work can be done in a way that matters.
The fourth asset is hope, and Duckworth is precise about what she means, because it is not the sunny kind.
The hope she is describing is not the feeling that tomorrow will probably be nicer.
It is the conviction that your own effort can change your future.
It is the belief that when you fall, you will get up, and that getting up will actually accomplish something.
To explain where that belief comes from, she goes back to one of the foundational experiments in modern psychology, the learned helplessness work by her mentor Martin Seligman and by Steven Maier.
In the original studies, animals given electric shocks they could not escape later failed to escape when escape became easy.
They simply lay down and took it.
They had learned, from experience, that their actions did not matter, and that lesson generalized to situations where it was no longer true.

The finding transformed the field, and much later Maier's neuroscience work refined it in a way I find hopeful: the passivity turns out to be the default response, and what is actually learned is control.
Learning that you have control is what changes the brain.
Two ideas grow directly out of this soil.
The first is Carol Dweck's work on mindset.
If you believe ability is fixed, a failure is a verdict about your ceiling, and the rational response to a verdict is to stop.
If you believe ability grows, a failure is information about the current gap, and the rational response is to work the gap.
The second is Seligman's work on explanatory style, on how we narrate bad events to ourselves.
The pessimistic style explains a setback with causes that are permanent and pervasive: I am bad at this, I am always bad at things like this.
The optimistic style explains it with causes that are temporary and specific: I did not put enough hours in this time, I misjudged the timing.
Both people experienced the same failure.
Only one of them retains a reason to try again next week.
And explanatory style, measured in advance, predicts who quits.
Duckworth's own life gives her the closing example here.
Her father's dinner-table verdict, you're no genius, was a claim about a fixed quantity.
Her whole career has been an argument that the interesting quantity is not fixed at all.
Now, having covered how grit grows from the inside, Duckworth spends the last third of the book on how it grows from the outside, from parents, from teachers and coaches, and from culture.
And she is refreshingly honest that the science here is younger and thinner than she would like.
The parenting question comes down to a false choice she wants to demolish.
Do you support your children, or do you demand things of them?
Warm, or tough?
The data say the answer is both, and that they are not on the same axis at all.
Psychologists map parenting on two dimensions, supportiveness and demandingness, which gives you four quadrants.
Demanding without support is authoritarian, and it produces compliance without confidence.
Supportive without demand is permissive, and it produces confidence without capability.
Neither is what you want.
What you want is what she calls wise parenting: highly supportive and highly demanding at the same time.
Warm, respectful, deeply aware of the child as a person, and also holding a standard and refusing to lower it.
Children raised that way, in study after study, do better on almost every outcome measured, including grit.

She also notes something that will comfort a lot of parents: the gritty people she interviewed frequently named a demanding parent or coach as formative, and just as frequently made clear that the demands only landed because they never doubted the person's love.
Judgment without warmth is just criticism.
Warmth without standards is just company.
Then there is her own family's rule, which is the single most portable idea in the book.
She and her husband instituted what they call the Hard Thing Rule, and it has three parts, and later a fourth.
Part one: everyone in the family, including both parents, has to do a hard thing.
A hard thing is defined as something that requires daily deliberate practice.
Her husband's is real estate development.
Hers is the psychology of grit.
The children pick their own.
Part two: you can quit.
This is the part people miss.
You are allowed to stop.
But you may not quit on a hard day.
You may not quit because your teacher shouted at you, or because you lost, or because you have a blister, or because it is boring today.
You can quit at a natural stopping point: the end of a season, the end of a term, the end of the tuition period you have paid for.
You finish what you signed up for, and then you are free.
Part three: you pick your own hard thing.
Nobody assigns it.
The interest has to be yours or none of the rest works.
And when her daughters reached high school she added a fourth: you must commit to at least one activity for at least two years.
That last part is not arbitrary.

It comes from research by Margo Gardner, following thousands of American teenagers into adulthood, which found that students who participated in extracurricular activities for two or more years, and made real progress in them, had substantially better outcomes later: they were more likely to graduate from college, more likely to be employed, earning more.
One year of an activity did not do it.
Follow-through did.

Duckworth's read is that these activities are one of the few places in modern life where a young person voluntarily takes on something difficult, with a demanding adult in charge, and sticks with it long enough to learn what sticking with something feels like.
Schools have tried to act on this, and Duckworth was close to one of the most interesting attempts.
She worked with Dave Levin, a co-founder of the KIPP charter school network, who had noticed a painful pattern in his own data.
KIPP had been extraordinarily successful at getting students from low-income neighborhoods into college.
But when they tracked those students through college, far too many did not finish.
And when Levin looked at which of his graduates did finish, the ones who made it were not reliably the ones who had the highest test scores.
They were the ones who had something else, some quality of persistence and optimism and social skill that nobody had been teaching on purpose.
So Levin, working with Duckworth and with Martin Seligman and with Dominic Randolph of the Riverdale Country School, built a character growth card.
Not a list of virtues on a poster, an actual report card, with specific observable behaviors, sent home alongside the academic grades.
They chose seven strengths, deliberately spanning all three of those clusters: grit, zest, self-control, optimism, gratitude, social intelligence, and curiosity.
And rather than rating a child as gritty or not, the indicators described behavior.
Finished whatever he began.
Kept working even after experiencing failure.
Came to class prepared.
Was eager to explore new things.
Duckworth is candid about the difficulty here.
Rating character has obvious hazards, teachers see only slices of a child, and there is real risk in reducing a human being to a score on a virtue.
But the underlying instinct she defends firmly: the things that determine how a life goes are being taught anyway, in every classroom and every household, just accidentally and invisibly.
Naming them at least lets you talk about them, and lets a child hear the specific sentence that changes so much, which is not you are talented, but you kept going.
Finally, culture.
Duckworth argues that the fastest way to change a person is to put them in a group where the thing you want them to be is simply what people are.
Not a rule they must follow, an identity they inhabit.

She spent time with Pete Carroll and the Seattle Seahawks while they were building a culture around competing in every single drill and finishing every rep. She looked at the Finnish idea of sisu, a national concept of stubborn inner strength in the face of impossible odds, and at West Point itself, where the culture is the actual curriculum.
Her point is that when grit is the norm, the individual does not need to summon it alone every morning.
You are simply the kind of person who does the hard thing, because that is what people around here do.
If you want to be grittier, one of the highest leverage moves available is to join a gritty group.
There is one more piece of evidence worth knowing, and it is the most encouraging in the book.
When Duckworth measured grit across thousands of American adults of different ages, she found that older people were, on average, grittier.
The sixty and seventy year olds scored higher than the twenty somethings, quite a lot higher.
Now, some of that could be a generational effect, people raised in harder times carrying different habits.

But it lines up with something personality researchers have documented for decades, called the maturity principle: across cultures, as people age, they tend to become more conscientious, more emotionally stable, more agreeable and more self-confident.
We do not stop developing at eighteen.
We change, mostly for the better, throughout adult life, largely because life keeps handing us circumstances that demand it and we keep rising to them.
Which means grit is not a fixed allotment you were handed at birth and have been spending ever since.
It grows.
Duckworth's own life is her exhibit A: she describes herself in her twenties as a serial quitter, cycling through jobs at a startling rate, and she can name the moment each interest ran out.
Her grit score today is high.
That is not because she was secretly gritty all along.
It is because she found a top-level goal worth organizing a life around, and everything else followed from that.

She also spends time on what she calls paragons of grit, the people she interviewed at the very top of their fields, and one of the things that struck her most was how little they talked about talent and how much they talked about time.
Will Smith gave her a line that has stuck with a lot of readers.
Asked to explain his success, he said he was not particularly gifted, but that if you and he got on treadmills together, only two things could happen: either you get off first, or he dies.
That is not a claim about ability.
It is a claim about willingness to keep going long past the point where the outcome stops being about ability at all.
And the paragons all described a relationship with failure that is worth naming, because it is very different from the way most of us hold it.
They did not describe themselves as unbothered by setbacks.
Several described being devastated.
What was different was the duration.
They spent a day, or a week, in the misery, and then returned.
Grit, in practice, is not the absence of the fall.
It is a short recovery time.
Now, I want to be honest with you about the limits of this book, because Duckworth is honest about them herself and because the argument has taken some fair criticism since it came out.
She says plainly that grit is not everything.

In her research on character, she describes at least three clusters: intrapersonal character, which is grit and self-control, the strengths of will; interpersonal character, which is gratitude, kindness, emotional intelligence, the strengths of heart; and intellectual character, which is curiosity and openness, the strengths of mind.
Grit sits in one of those three boxes.
A person can be enormously gritty and also selfish, or cruel, or narrow.
She says she would not want that for her children and does not want you to read her book as a claim that persistence is the highest human value.
She also warns explicitly against the misuse of the idea.
Grit is not a reason to tell a struggling person that their circumstances are their fault.
Talent, opportunity, money, health and luck are all real, and no questionnaire changes that.

And she has been publicly uneasy about schools using her scale to grade children or about anyone using it in hiring, for the very good reason that a twelve item self-report about how persistent you are is trivially easy to fake when something is riding on the answer.
It is a mirror, not a filter.
Finally, the size of the effect is real but human-sized.
Grit predicted survival at Beast Barracks better than the West Point score did, which is remarkable given how much work went into that score.
It did not predict it perfectly, and Duckworth does not claim it did.
What she claims is that we have spent a century measuring how fast people learn and almost no time measuring how long they stay, and that the second thing turns out to matter enormously.
So let me pull the whole thing together.
Achievement is not a single quantity.
It is talent multiplied by effort to produce skill, and then skill multiplied by effort again to produce accomplishment, which means the hours count twice and the gift counts once.
We prefer the story of the natural because it flatters us and lets us off, and even trained experts fall for it when you attach the right backstory to an identical recording.
Excellence itself, looked at up close, turns out to be mundane: dozens of small, ordinary, learnable things done correctly and consistently until they stack.
The people who accumulate those hours are not made of different stuff.
They have built four things.
An interest that was triggered by accident and then deepened over years of return visits, not a passion found in a single revelation.
A practice habit aimed squarely at their weakest point, with immediate feedback, done as a daily ritual so it does not require a decision.
A purpose that connects the work to other people, which is what keeps you there when the interest alone runs dry.

And a hope that is not optimism about the weather but the specific conviction that your effort changes outcomes, built from a growth mindset and a habit of explaining setbacks as temporary and specific rather than permanent and total.

And all of that can be grown from the outside as well as the inside, by parents and coaches who are demanding and warm at the same time, by a family rule that says you may quit but not on a bad day, and by joining a culture where doing hard things is simply what people here do.
The line Duckworth returns to, borrowed from one of her gritty subjects, is that this is about living life like a marathon, not a sprint.
Not the heroic burst.
The long, unglamorous, cumulative haul, which is available to far more people than the story of talent ever admitted.
So let me leave you with the practical heart of it, the things you can do this week.

Take the Grit Scale honestly, and pay particular attention to the passion half rather than the perseverance half, because most people who score low score low there, on consistency of interests over years, not on effort in a given month.
If you have restarted from scratch every eighteen months, that is the thing to look at.
Stop waiting to discover your passion and start deliberately dabbling instead.
Pick two or three things that are mildly more interesting than the rest and give each of them real, repeated exposure over months rather than a single trial.
Interest deepens with knowledge, so the boredom you feel at the start is usually a lack of expertise, not a lack of fit.
Build one ritual of deliberate practice.
Same time, same place, every day, aimed at the specific part of your work you are currently worst at, with some source of immediate honest feedback.
Expect it to feel bad.
That feeling is the sensation of improvement, not the sensation of being unsuited.
Write down your goal hierarchy.
List the things you are working toward, then ask of each one, why am I doing this, until you arrive at the small number of top-level goals that everything else serves.
Then look hard at what is on the list that serves nothing at the top, and cut it.
Find the beyond-yourself part of your work and make it explicit.
Ask who is actually better off because you did this well, and if the honest answer is nobody, either craft the job so that changes or take that seriously as information.
Change how you narrate your failures.

When something goes wrong, catch the permanent, pervasive explanation, I am bad at this, and deliberately replace it with the temporary, specific one, I have not put in enough reps on this particular thing yet.
And adopt some version of the Hard Thing Rule, for yourself and for anyone you are raising.
Pick a hard thing that needs daily practice, choose it yourself, and give yourself full permission to quit, but only at the end of a season, never on a bad day.
Almost every abandoned pursuit in a human life was abandoned on a bad day.
